subtype: Parent fighting with a sleepy teen [Receiver]
passage:
Monday, at dawn: "Tushar! Third time! Up!" Rajni pounded on his door. A grunt. Then the bathroom door slammed, and mother and son left the house without a kind word.
Thursday evening: Rajni sat on the end of his bed. "I'm tired of fighting. I read that teenagers' bodies want to sleep later. What would help?" Tushar blinked, surprised. They agreed his phone would charge in the hall at night, and he would wake to his own alarm at the same time every day, weekends included.
The next Monday: his alarm rang once. Tushar shuffled into the kitchen, hair wild, and muttered, "Morning." Rajni passed him his tea. No doors slammed.

qa.q: Where does Tushar's phone charge at night after the deal?
qa.a: In the hall.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling on the first Monday when he slammed the door?
qa.a: He felt angry and cornered; being shouted awake while groggy made him defensive.

qa.q: What changed on Thursday, and why did it work better than shouting?
qa.a: Rajni talked calmly and asked what would help, and they agreed on a phone rule and a steady wake time; Tushar had a say, so he kept to it.

qa.q: How were the early mornings affecting Rajni at first?
qa.a: She was frustrated and worn down, calling three times and starting her own day angry.

grounding: Shows a parent's dawn shouting drawing grunts and slammed doors, and a calm talk about teen sleep leading to agreed phone and wake-up rules.

subtype: Parent fighting with a sleepy teen [Receiver]
passage: Rashmi, you shout at your son Aman every morning the way I, Rajni, once shouted at your brother Deepak. I'd stand at his door at dawn: "Up! Up! Are you a buffalo?" He'd grunt, the door would slam twice, and neither of us said a kind word before school. One day his teacher told me many teenagers simply can't fall asleep early; their bodies run later. I thought it was an excuse. Still, one Sunday I stopped yelling and sat down with Deepak. We agreed the radio went off after dinner and he'd wake at the same time every day, even holidays, with his own clock. He grumbled, but the slamming stopped. We started talking again at breakfast.

qa.q: What did Rajni used to shout at Deepak's door?
qa.a: "Up! Up! Are you a buffalo?"

qa.q: What did Rajni feel when the teacher explained teen sleep?
qa.a: She felt doubtful, even dismissive, thinking it was just an excuse.

qa.q: What was the turning point with Deepak, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Rajni stopped yelling and sat down with him to agree on the radio going off after dinner and a steady wake time; he had a say, so the slamming stopped.

qa.q: How might those dawn shouts have felt to Deepak?
qa.a: Harsh and humiliating when he was already groggy, which is why he answered with grunts and slammed doors.

grounding: Illustrates a parent learning that shouting at a sleepy teen breeds slammed doors, while understanding and a negotiated routine repair the relationship.

subtype: Parent fighting with a sleepy teen [Receiver]
passage: In their Nashik flat the tap water came only from six to seven, and every morning Jatin needed Nilesh up to fill the drums. "Nilesh! Six o'clock! Get up!" A grunt. At 6:20 Jatin banged on the door. "Useless boy!" Nilesh stumbled out, filled one drum in silence, and slammed the bathroom door so hard a bucket toppled. That night, after a colleague mentioned how teenagers' sleep runs late, Jatin knocked softly. "Can we make a deal? You're up at 6:15, and no shouting from me. Your phone goes to the hall at 10:30." Nilesh looked at him for a long second. "And no 'useless'?" "No 'useless'." The next morning at 6:15, Nilesh was at the tap, yawning, but talking.

qa.q: When did the tap water come?
qa.a: From six to seven.

qa.q: What does Nilesh's question, "And no 'useless'?", reveal?
qa.a: He had been hurt by the word more than by being woken, and he wanted to feel respected as part of the deal.

qa.q: Why did the deal work better than banging on the door?
qa.a: It set a steady wake time and a phone cut-off both could agree on, and dropping the insult protected their relationship.

qa.q: How does Jatin see the morning fights after talking to his colleague?
qa.a: He begins to see Nilesh's grunts as partly sleepiness rather than laziness, and chooses a deal over shouting.

grounding: Shows a teen on the receiving end of dawn shouting, and a parent who learns about teen sleep and negotiates a phone cut-off and steady wake time.

subtype: Parent fighting with a sleepy teen [Receiver]
passage: Every morning in their Kolkata flat began the same way: Madhuri at Saurabh's door at 5:30, calling his name every two minutes, and Saurabh growling "Five more" into the pillow. On Tuesday he threw his pillow at the door. Madhuri shouted back, and they didn't speak all day. That night she found him at his desk, not studying, just staring. "Why can't you sleep earlier?" she asked, tired now rather than angry. "I try, Ma. My body isn't sleepy till twelve." She thought about that. "Then let's change the plan. You set your own alarm, I stop calling. Screens off at 10:30. Sundays you sleep late." Saurabh blinked. "Seriously?" "Seriously. I'm tired of fighting you." On Wednesday the alarm rang, and he got up on the second snooze. Nobody shouted.

qa.q: What time did Madhuri come to Saurabh's door each morning?
What was Saurabh feeling when he threw his pillow at the door?
qa.a: He felt irritated and cornered, pulled out of sleep by constant calling when his body had not been sleepy until midnight.

qa.q: What made the new plan protect their relationship?
qa.a: It swapped nagging for a fair deal: his own alarm, screens off at 10:30 and Sunday lie-ins, so the dawn fights stopped.

qa.q: How had the mornings affected Madhuri?
qa.a: She was worn out and angry, then simply tired of fighting her son, which opened her to a new plan.

grounding: Shows a teen and parent locked in dawn nagging and slammed responses, and a negotiated plan on screens and wake time easing it.

subtype: Parent fighting with a sleepy teen [Receiver]
passage:
"Yash! Bus in ten minutes!"
"Mmph."
"Third time this week I'm driving you! Get up!"
A door slammed.
That evening:
"Papa, can I say something? When I was sixteen, I couldn't sleep before one either."
"Divyansh, you were lazy too."
"Maybe. But teenage body clocks really do shift later. Shouting at six just gets you slammed doors."
"So what, I let him sleep till nine?"
"No. Make a deal with him."
Later, at Yash's door:
"Yash, I'm sorry about this morning. Can we try something? Phone charges in the kitchen at ten-thirty. Same wake-up time every day, a bit later on Sundays."
"And no shouting?"
"One knock. Then the curtains open."
"Okay. Deal."

qa.q: How many times had Papa driven Yash to school that week?
qa.a: It was the third time that week.

qa.q: What did Yash want when asking, "And no shouting?"
qa.a: Yash wanted respect; the shouting at six had left Yash feeling attacked, and Yash was wary it would go on.

qa.q: What made Papa's evening approach better than the morning one?
qa.a: He apologised and offered a clear deal on phone time and a steady wake-up, which protects the relationship instead of starting another fight.

qa.q: How does Divyansh see the dawn fights?
qa.a: Divyansh sees them from experience: a sleepy teen, not only a lazy one, and shouting that only brings slammed doors.

grounding: Shows a teen receiving dawn shouting, and a parent who learns about teen body clocks negotiating a phone cut-off and a steady wake time instead.

subtype: Parent fighting with a sleepy teen [Receiver]
passage: Every morning last term began with me shouting at Aditi's door at six. 'Get up! You'll miss the van!' And every morning I got grunts, a slammed door and a girl who wouldn't look at me over breakfast. My neighbour laughed, 'Usha, your flat sounds like a war.' I thought my daughter had turned lazy and rude. Then, waiting at the dentist's, I read that teenagers' body clocks shift later, so they genuinely can't fall asleep early. I felt ashamed of all the shouting. That evening I asked Aditi what might help instead of ordering her. We agreed on phones charging in the hall by ten-thirty and the same wake-up time every day, even Sundays. I bought her a loud alarm clock and stopped being her alarm. Mornings are still slow, but we talk again.

qa.q: What time do the phones go to charge in the hall?
qa.a: By ten-thirty.

qa.q: How did Usha feel after reading about teenagers' body clocks?
qa.a: Usha felt ashamed of all the shouting, realising Aditi genuinely couldn't fall asleep early.

qa.q: What agreement did Usha and Aditi reach?
qa.a: Phones charging in the hall by ten-thirty, the same wake-up time daily, and a loud alarm clock instead of Usha's shouting.

qa.q: How might Aditi have experienced those shouting mornings?
qa.a: Aditi probably felt exhausted and attacked, which came out as grunts and slammed doors.

grounding: A parent who shouts at a sleepy teenager learns about body clocks and negotiates phone cut-offs and a steady wake time.
